entries.title: Pyu · urban communities
entries.note: Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra preserve a long sequence of walled settlements, water management, Buddhist institutions and exchange. This is an archaeological urban tradition, not evidence for one empire with fixed borders. Rounded century limits describe the documented sequence.

entries.title: Bagan · imperial and temple-building phase
entries.note: The Bagan landscape records a major Buddhist capital and regional empire. The range marks its best-known monumental and imperial phase, not the full occupation of the city or the beginning of Burmese history.

entries.title: Toungoo · expanding and restored courts
entries.location: Myanmar and changing areas of mainland Southeast Asia
entries.note: A dynastic umbrella for an initially local court, sixteenth-century imperial expansion and a smaller restored kingdom. The late-sixteenth-century collapse and subsequent restoration interrupt any simple picture of continuous territorial control. Shan, Mon and neighbouring powers retained distinct histories.

entries.title: Konbaung dynasty
entries.note: Konbaung kings expanded their realm and later lost territory in successive wars with British forces. British capture of Mandalay and exile of King Thibaw in 1885 ended the dynasty; formal annexation of Upper Burma followed in 1886.

entries.title: Burma · British expansion and colonial rule
entries.note: British rule spread in stages after the wars of 1824–1826, 1852–1853 and 1885. These dates do not imply the whole present-day country was colonised in 1826. Japanese occupation interrupted British control during the Second World War; independence followed in January 1948.

entries.title: Myanmar / Burma · independent state
entries.note: Independence on 4 January 1948 anchors this modern-state entry. Its broad span includes major changes in government and continuing conflicts; it does not imply an unchanged constitution, uniform central control or the disappearance of the country’s many peoples.

entries.title: Dvaravati · towns and cultural networks
entries.location: Central and northeastern present-day Thailand and adjoining areas
entries.note: Buddhist monuments, inscriptions and material culture link several early urban centres. Dvaravati is treated here as a cultural and political network rather than one securely bounded empire. Individual sites and traditions flourished at different times within this approximate range.

entries.title: Sukhothai kingdom
entries.note: An important court and group of towns supported Buddhist architecture and ceramics. The conventional kingdom range includes later dependence on Ayutthaya before annexation; it is not a claim that all of present-day Thailand was unified under Sukhothai.

entries.title: Ayutthaya kingdom
entries.location: Chao Phraya basin and changing tributary networks
entries.note: Ayutthaya became a major diplomatic and commercial capital. Sources use 1350 or 1351 for its founding. Its reach changed over time; the Burmese destruction of the capital in 1767 ended this ruling phase, not Siamese society.

entries.title: Thonburi kingdom
entries.note: King Taksin established a court at Thonburi after Ayutthaya’s fall and reconsolidated power amid competing regional centres. Bangkok became the new royal capital under Rama I in 1782.

entries.title: Siam / Thailand · Bangkok and constitutional eras
entries.note: The Bangkok era began in 1782. Absolute monarchy ended in 1932, followed by successive constitutional and military governments. The name Thailand was adopted in 1939, with a later temporary return to Siam; neither the name change nor 1782 marks the beginning of the region’s peoples.

entries.title: Champa · changing Cham polities
entries.location: Coastal central and southern present-day Vietnam
entries.note: Champa comprised changing regional centres and principalities rather than an unchanging nation-state. My Son preserves major religious monuments; southern Panduranga outlasted the fall of Vijaya in 1471 and was absorbed by the Nguyễn state in 1832. Cham people and cultural traditions continue.

entries.title: Chăm communities · living histories
entries.note: Cham history continues beyond the loss of independent principalities. Living pottery traditions in Vietnam, passed on within families and communities, offer one documented example. This entry does not assign a single founding date to a diverse people or reduce Cham life to a former kingdom.

entries.title: Butuan · maritime communities and boat-building
entries.note: Excavated lashed-lug boats attest to sophisticated boat-building and maritime connections. This selected range dates the boat evidence identified by the National Museum, not the fixed lifespan or borders of a supposed kingdom. Settlement and trade at Butuan extended beyond it.

entries.title: Sulu sultanate · political authority
entries.location: Sulu Archipelago and changing maritime networks
entries.note: A Muslim sultanate developed within older island trading societies. Its autonomy contracted under Spanish and American expansion; the 1915 agreement ended the sultan’s temporal sovereignty. Religious authority, communities and contested later claims have separate histories, and 1915 does not mark their disappearance.

entries.title: Philippines · Spanish colonial rule
entries.note: Permanent Spanish settlement began in 1565; colonial rule expanded unevenly and faced continuing Indigenous and Muslim resistance. The revolution and the 1898 transfer claimed by Spain and the United States did not amount to a consensual transfer of every community’s sovereignty.

entries.title: Philippines · revolution, U.S. rule and war
entries.note: Filipino revolutionaries asserted independence and founded the First Republic while the United States imposed colonial rule. The Commonwealth began in 1935; Japanese invasion and occupation interrupted American administration. The United States formally recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946.

entries.title: Philippines · independent republic
entries.note: The 1946 date marks internationally recognised independence after American colonial rule. The earlier 1898 declaration remains commemorated as Independence Day. A single modern-state entry cannot stand for every Indigenous nation, regional community or constitutional era within the archipelago.

entries.title: Melaka · Malay sultanate and trading port
entries.note: A Malay sultanate made Melaka an important multicultural trading port. Portuguese conquest in 1511 ended this selected ruling phase; the city and regional Malay courts continued under changing conditions. This is not a continuous empire connecting Srivijaya directly to Malaysia.

entries.title: Malaysia · federation
entries.note: Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963 from Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore. Malaya had gained independence in 1957; Singapore separated in 1965. The federation’s formation does not date the beginnings of its many Indigenous, Malay, Chinese, Indian and other communities.

entries.title: Singapore · independent republic
entries.note: Singapore became a sovereign republic on 9 August 1965 after separation from Malaysia. Earlier Temasek, Malay and regional histories, the British settlement from 1819, wartime occupation and self-government preceded this modern-state phase.

entries.title: Brunei Darussalam · full independence
entries.note: Full independence resumed on 1 January 1984, ending British responsibility for external affairs and defence. This date identifies the contemporary sovereign-state phase, not the origin of the much older Brunei sultanate or its people.

entries.title: Lan Xang kingdom
entries.location: Mekong region · mainly present-day Laos and adjoining areas
entries.note: Lan Xang developed around interconnected courts and Buddhist centres, including Luang Prabang and later Vientiane. Internal divisions and external pressures changed royal power; partition produced distinct successor kingdoms. Its territory and communities do not map directly onto modern national borders.

entries.title: Laos · independence and republic
entries.note: The 1953 treaty removed the remaining French restrictions on independence, following earlier autonomy within the French Union. Civil war and extensive bombing shaped later decades. The monarchy ended with proclamation of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic in 1975.

entries.title: Timor-Leste · restored independence
entries.location: Eastern Timor, Oecusse and neighbouring islands
entries.note: Independence was declared in 1975, followed by Indonesian invasion and occupation. The 1999 referendum led to a United Nations-administered transition and restoration of independence on 20 May 2002. This modern-state date does not begin Timorese history.

entries.title: Karen communities · living heritage
entries.note: Karen is an umbrella for diverse communities rather than one state or uniform identity. Weaving, language, ecological knowledge and community institutions continue across borders and displacement. The selected sources document people sustaining these traditions today; no single origin date is assigned.
